newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian army parade honours bid for independence.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian army parade honours bid for independence.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem commanders staged a vast military parade on Tuesday to honour the army that fought to save Bosnia's independence.
Some 35,000 people turned out to see columns of soldiers march to the strains of patriotic anthems in a Sarajevo soccer stadium.
Moslem political and military leaders said the army had served heroically and stood as a deterrent to any potential foe.
"The people are proud of you. They know that you are the best soldiers in the world and you really are," said Alija Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of the peacetime collective presidency.
"The enemy knows that, and next time they will think twice before they dare to raise a hand against this country and its people."
Some 2,500 soldiers and a row of wounded veterans in wheelchairs watched as Izetbegovic pinned a medal on the army's wartime commander, General Rasim Delic.
Delic said the Bosnian army had "prevented the disappearance of one people, Bosniaks (Moslems), and one country, Bosnia-Herzegovina".
The army formed by the Bosnian government during the 1992-95 war eventually became identified as a mainly Moslem force fighting against Serb separatists and later Croat separatists.
The Bosnian army was heavily outgunned by Serb forces during most of the war, suffering heavy losses as it tried to break the Serb siege of the capital Sarajevo.
Bosnian Croat and Moslem leaders have agreed to form a joint army as part of a Moslem-Croat federation, which covers half the country under a peace treaty signed in December 1995.
The United States has tied a military aid programme to progress in creating a unifed federation army.
A joint command has been established after lengthy negotiations and Croat and Moslem brigades are supposed to gradually merge over a three-year period.
Izetbegovic, who served as Bosnia's wartime president, said the Bosnian army had helped preserve the country's multi-ethnic character.
"Where ever you were -- mosques, churches, cathedrals and synagogues remained. This is your and our biggest victory."
The NATO-led peace force waived restrictions on weapons and allowed soldiers in the parade to carry rifles.
